bridge: Builds on B03 API schema and S06 ownership. Use this complete invented object dataset.
teaching:
API security begins with a contract for object identifiers, properties and operations. Object-level access decides which row a caller may touch. Property-level access decides which fields may be read or changed. A valid object id does not authorise every field update.

Mass assignment happens when a server blindly applies supplied fields to its internal object. Define writable fields explicitly and derive protected fields such as owner or role from trusted state. Schema validation should reject unexpected types, unknown operations and oversized collections.

Documentation helps reviewers find intended endpoints but does not itself enforce them. Test every operation with owner, non-owner and unauthenticated identities. Include a positive case so that returning errors for every request cannot masquerade as a working authorisation system.
example:
Objects: n1={owner:A,body:"one"}; n2={owner:B,body:"two"}
PATCH /notes/{id}: body field only; max100 chars
A PATCH n1 {body:"new"} -> allow
A PATCH n2 {body:"new"} -> deny ownership
A PATCH n1 {owner:"B"}  -> reject protected field
A PATCH n1 {body:7}     -> reject type
No identity PATCH n1   -> deny authentication
explanation: The ownership decision uses the stored object and authenticated principal. Rejecting an owner field prevents the request from changing the very state used to authorise it. The policy can consistently reject all unknown keys rather than silently accepting misspellings.
exercise: Build the five-case test matrix above and add B reading n2, B reading n1 and A updating a101-character body. Identify whether each failure is authentication, object access or schema validation.
solution: A PATCH n1 with a string body is allowed. A PATCH n2 fails object access. A supplying owner fails the writable-field schema. A supplying body 7 fails type validation. No-identity PATCH fails authentication. Added cases: B reading n2 is allowed; B reading n1 fails object access; A updating n1 with 101 characters fails the 100-character limit. Check both returned response and stored object: denied cases must leave it unchanged.
challenge: Add an internal audit_only field that ordinary users cannot read. Define response fields and update fields separately, then describe how you would test that a normal GET does not expose audit_only.
challenge_solution: One policy returns only id and body on ordinary GET; owner may be used internally without being returned, and audit_only is never included. The PATCH writable allowlist contains only body. Given n1 with audit_only="internal-demo", test that A’s GET includes the expected body but no audit_only key, that A cannot PATCH audit_only, and that B cannot GET n1 at all. Inspect the raw JSON response as well as the visible UI; hiding a received field does not protect it.
